messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kenji, a gentle, 55-year-old man from Guam who had made his life in the States, described the moment his world fractured with a quiet, halting voice. Eight months ago, he was watching his four-year-old grandson, Leo, in the backyard. It was a sun-drenched Saturday, the kind he used to cherish. Leo, a whirlwind of energy, was climbing the old oak tree, something Kenji had cautioned him about but had never strictly forbidden. He had turned away for just a moment to answer his phone when he heard the sickening thud. The image of Leo’s small, twisted body on the grass, one arm bent at an unnatural angle, was seared into his mind. He remembers the high-pitched wail that he later realized was his own, a sound that now sometimes echoes in his head when the house is too quiet. Leo survived, but with lasting injuries, and Kenji’s life has been a ruin ever since.

The memory of that day is not a coherent story he can tell. When he tries to explain to his daughter or his ex-wife what happened, the words tangle in his throat and the thread is lost. It comes back to him in vicious, sensory fragments. The memory of the fall, and the overwhelming grief that accompanies it, inevitably gives way to a crushing sense of personal failure. He is no longer just a grandfather who witnessed a tragic accident; in his own mind, he is the man who failed to protect the most precious person in his life. This core belief—"I should have protected him and I failed"—has become the lens through which he views himself. He feels he is fundamentally a weak person, someone who froze when he should have acted, who faltered when strength was required.

This profound sense of failure has, in turn, reshaped the memory itself. His belief that he is weak and incompetent pulls certain details into sharp focus while blurring others. He no longer remembers the minutes leading up to the fall, only the instant he looked away. The memory replays not as a sequence of events, but as a referendum on his character. The sound he hears is not just Leo’s cry but the sound of his own inadequacy. This self-recrimination makes him feel hollowed out, less like a person and more like an object defined only by his catastrophic mistake. This feeling of being dehumanized, of being just the vessel for this failure, has made him retreat from his family, convinced they see him the same way.

His work as a nanny for a wealthy family has become a form of daily torture. His conviction that he failed to protect Leo has made him hyper-attuned to any reminder of his grandson or the accident. These triggers are no longer neutral; they are personal accusations. When the two young children he cares for run through the living room, he feels a jolt of panic. The sight of their small hands reaching for his is particularly potent, a visual echo of Leo’s own hands that he now sees as fragile and vulnerable because of him. At the park, when he overhears other parents or nannies discussing a child’s scraped knee or a close call at the playground, he feels a hot flush of shame. These conversations about loss or potential loss feel like a direct commentary on his own unforgivable lapse. He has started making excuses to avoid the park, keeping the children inside more often, a change the parents have begun to notice and question.

He came to therapy because his daughter, seeing him so withdrawn and tormented, insisted. He is terrified of losing his job, his only source of income since his divorce, but more than that, he is terrified that he is right. He is afraid that he truly is a weak man who cannot be trusted, and that he is doomed to live out his days as a ghost, haunted by the memory of the day he failed. He wants to be able to see his grandson without feeling like a criminal, but the hope that he might one day forgive himself feels impossibly distant.
